chapter_theme: The closing summary (கட்டுரை) of the Madurai book: one long sentence lists what the book set out about the Pandya line and its land (righteousness, valour, the old city, festivals, the gods' visits, the Vaigai's plenty, the unfailing sky, the two dramatic modes and the vari and kuravai songs) and says the book lies viewed as one with the Pandya Nedunjeliyan, victor over the northern Aryan armies, who slept on his royal couch with his queen of flawless chastity.

silappathikaram:madurai_kandam_katturai:.reading: The narrator closes the Madurai book by gathering into one view the righteousness, valour and strength of the Pandya line among the three crowned kings, their old city, its festivals and divine visitors, the people and harvests of their land, the Vaigai that feeds it, the sky that never fails its rain, the two modes of drama and the vari and kuravai songs, all seen together with Nedunjeliyan, who defeated the northern Aryan armies and, before all the Tamil south, came to lie still on his throne-couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
silappathikaram:madurai_kandam_katturai:.nuance: The opening lines repeat, nearly word for word, the frame that closes the Puhar book, with the Vaigai for the Kaveri; so the praise of aram and of a sky that never fails (பொய்யா வானம், line 9) is given to the very line whose king the book has shown condemning an innocent man, and the summary does not take it back. The book's judgment shows only at the close, where the whole book is set beside a death: துஞ்சிய (line 17), 'slept', is the courtly word for a king's dying, and the queen's death at his feet (20:88-91) becomes a shared lying on the royal couch. The summary gives the epithet of flawless chastity (புரைதீர் கற்பின்) to the Pandya's queen, and does not name Kannaki, Kovalan or the burning of the city at all. The epithet வடஆரியர் படைகடந்து (line 14) matches the name under which tradition files Purananuru 183 (ஆரியப் படை கடந்த நெடுஞ்செழியன்); the Tamil here gives the epithet, not a proof that the two are one king, so no link is built on it. Lines 10 to 13 name two dramatic modes (ஆரபடி, சாத்துவதி) and the songs and say they appear together 'with other matter set in' (பிறபொருள் வைப்போடு); the reading does not turn on the technical terms.

links.note: The verdict scene ends with the Pandya saying 'am I king? I am the thief', falling dead, and his queen falling at his feet saying there is nothing to show those who have lost their husbands; the summary recalls this as the king who slept on his throne-couch with his queen of flawless chastity.
links.teaches: The summary turns the king's self-condemnation and his wife's instant death into one dignified image of a royal pair at rest, and gives its only epithet of chastity to the queen and does not name Kannaki, so the book's official memory honours the Pandya's atoning death as the thing its whole story is viewed with.

links.note: The couplet says that if the ruler bends justice the sky, bending its rain, will not pour; the summary credits the Pandya land, whose king bent justice in this book, with a sky that never fails to pour new rain.
links.teaches: Read against the couplet, the summary's line of unfailing rain claims for the Pandya land the very sign the Kural withdraws from a bent sceptre, so the epic's punishment for the bent sceptre falls on the king's own life and the city by fire rather than on the rain, and its stock praise of the land survives the verdict intact.

gains.a: the formula line about rain gains a political charge: under the couplet it is a claim that the king ruled justly, which the book itself has refuted
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the bent sceptre is answered by a different penalty than drought, the king's death and his city's burning, which limits the couplet's rain as the only sign of misrule

links.note: Bhoothapandiyan's queen rebukes the elders who hold her back and chooses the pyre over the widow's austerities, calling fire and a lotus pond one to her; the summary sets the Pandya Nedunjeliyan's queen of flawless chastity lying with him on the throne-couch, her death having come at once at his feet.
links.teaches: Both remember a Pandya queen who would not outlive her husband, but the Puram queen must argue her way to the pyre against counsel, while the epic's queen dies without fire or argument and the summary counts that death as flawless chastity, so together they show the widow's death moving from a chosen and contested act to a sign of karpu that needs no choosing.

gains.a: the summary's praise of the queen gains the older Pandya precedent of a wife who refused widowhood, which shows what kind of chastity புரைதீர் கற்பின் is honouring
gains.b: the Puram poem gains a later version of its scene in which no elders object and no pyre is needed, which shows the queen's resolve becoming an ideal assumed rather than argued

source_issues: Lines 14, 15, 18 and 19 are short lines inside the akaval frame (வடஆரியர் படைகடந்து, தென்றமிழ்நா டொருங்குகாணப், நெடுஞ்செழியனோ டொருபரிசா, நோக்கிக் கிடந்த); the Puhar and Vanchi summaries built on the same frame have full lines here, so the edition's line division may differ from the metre.

Line 6 reads அவருடை நாட்டுக் where the Vanchi summary has அவருறை நாட்டுக்; line 18 reads ஒருபரிசா where the Vanchi summary has ஒருபரிசு நோக்கி. Either may be a variant or a misprint; the sense is unaffected.
Line 20 (மதுரைக் காண்டம் முற்றிற்று) is a colophon that also completes the sentence (கிடந்த governs காண்டம்), so it is marked as part of the unit.
